issues.legal_issue: Good-faith acts and omissions by officials administering an estate-management law are protected from tort damages unless the loss was caused by an officer’s wilful default or gross negligence.
material_facts: The State took over management of an estate under a statute and appointed a government officer as its manager.
The owner alleged losses arising from the partial notification of estate interests, delayed preparation of collection papers, collection proceedings, and failures to pursue pending proceedings.

The owner did not provide the requested records and collection papers until several months after the request; the manager had sought notification of the remaining interests after the error was raised, and a supplementary notification was issued.
A large number of collection cases were filed hurriedly on the basis of an arrears list supplied by the owner, and the management was relinquished within months.
The Court found no proof that the State or its officers acted dishonestly, deliberately abused statutory power, or caused loss through wilful default or gross negligence.
issues.conclusion: The statutory protection applied to the claims for damages based on the officials’ acts and omissions. The evidence did not establish wilful default or gross negligence, so those claims failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Bihar State Management of Estates and Tenures Act, 1949 bars proceedings concerning acts done or purporting to be done in good faith under the Act, and concerning alleged neglect, omissions, or exercise or non-exercise of statutory powers, except for loss caused by an officer’s wilful default or gross negligence. Under section 4(22) of the Bihar and Orissa General Clauses Act, 1917, an act is done in good faith if it is done honestly, whether negligently or not. The Court also applied the statutory provisions allowing notification of a fraction of a tenure and requiring the proprietor to provide records requested for management. It referred to State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga (1952 SCR 889) in discussing the reform purpose of the management legislation.

rule.if: tort_damages_proceeding and statutory_estate_management and acts_done_honestly and not loss_caused_by_wilful_default_or_gross_negligence

predicates.tort_damages_proceeding: A claimant brings a tort damages proceeding against a public authority or its officers over the management of an estate.
predicates.statutory_estate_management: The public authority and its officers acted or omitted to act while administering an estate under statutory management powers.
predicates.acts_done_honestly: The authority or its officers acted honestly in carrying out the management, even if an act or omission may have been negligent.
predicates.loss_caused_by_wilful_default_or_gross_n: An officer’s wilful default or gross negligence caused the loss claimed.

issues.definition: When a tort damages proceeding concerns statutory estate management, the acts were done honestly, and wilful default or gross negligence did not cause the loss, the damages claim is barred.

issues.legal_issue: The State must reimburse management expenditure that exceeded the amount authorized for management where its manager offered to refund the excess.
material_facts: During the short period of government management, management expenses exceeded the authorized level by approximately Rs. 8,000.
The manager had offered to refund any expenditure exceeding 25 per cent of gross collections.
issues.conclusion: The State was liable to repay the management expenditure incurred in excess of what was authorized.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the excess management expenditure was beyond what was authorized by law and relied on the manager’s offer to refund expenditure exceeding 25 per cent of gross collections. It ordered repayment of the excess with interest.

predicates.statutory_estate_management: The State managed an estate under statutory authority.
predicates.management_expense_exceeded_authorized_l: The expenditure incurred for management exceeded the amount authorized for that management.
predicates.manager_offered_to_refund_excess: The manager offered to repay management expenditure exceeding the stated share of gross collections.

issues.definition: If statutory estate management incurred expenses beyond the authorized limit and the manager offered to refund the excess, the State must reimburse the excess management expense.

issues.legal_issue: The State is not liable to reimburse a tax penalty where the management notification was authorized and the penalty is too remote from the management.
material_facts: A penalty was imposed because agricultural income tax was not paid on time, and it was later reduced on appeal.
The owner attributed the penalty to the State’s failure to collect arrears in time.
The Court held that the initial notification placing part of the estate under management was authorized and that the penalty was too remote from the manager’s conduct.
issues.conclusion: The State was not liable to reimburse the tax penalty.
issues.legal_principle: The Court concluded that, because the initial notification was authorized, the State could not be held liable for reimbursing the penalty; it also found the penalty too remote from the management of the notified estate. The general statutory protection against claims for acts and omissions under the management law was addressed under section 31 of the Bihar State Management of Estates and Tenures Act, 1949.

rule.if: tort_damages_proceeding and tax_penalty_claim and initial_notification_authorized and penalty_too_remote_from_statutory_management

predicates.tort_damages_proceeding: A claimant seeks damages from the State for conduct connected with statutory estate management.
predicates.tax_penalty_claim: The claimant seeks reimbursement of a penalty imposed for failing to pay a tax on time.
predicates.initial_notification_authorized: The initial notification placing estate interests under government management was authorized.
predicates.penalty_too_remote_from_statutory_manage: The tax penalty was too remote from the government officer’s management of the estate.

issues.definition: When a tort damages proceeding includes a tax-penalty claim, the initial management notification was authorized, and the penalty is too remote from statutory management, the State is not liable to reimburse the penalty.
